english.html: history does not name, calling himself the son of Cn. Asinius Dio, came within a little, in the time of Cornelius Sulla, of causing the true child of Asinius Dio to be deprived of his father's goods: for he had so well trained the artillery of his stratagems that judgment had followed in his favour. But Augustus Caesar, a wise, prudent and fortunate prince and emperor, having subtly brought the imposture to light, caused the property to be restored to the legitimate son, and the cheat to die in prison <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. At the same time, in the city of Milan, a very wealthy woman called Rubria was burnt to death by a great disaster; after whose death, when her heirs had already sold the better part of the property, another woman presented herself, calling herself Rubria, demanding that her property be restored to her; whom several even of Augustus's soldiers supported, persuaded, by the likeness she bore both in face and in manners to the deceased, that she was truly Rubria. But the incomparable prudence of that renowned and generous Emperor prevented the execution of the fraud. <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>

notes.citation: Valerius Maximus IX.15 again (printed ſ. xvi for c. xvi), the false son of Cn. Asinius Dio (fragment number unverified)

notes.gloss: Coras's Cn. Assidio is Valerius's Cn. Asinius Dio. Valerius has the cause won under Sulla and overturned by Augustus's judgment, as Coras tells it; the pretender died in prison.

notes.citation: Valerius Maximus IX.15, the false Rubria of Milan (fragment number unverified)

notes.gloss: Valerius has Calca pretending to be Clodius himself and suing for his estate before the centumviral court; Coras makes him Clodius's son.

english.html: Which property this same du Tilh had since sold to several and divers persons.

From this fact a question may arise in the future: whether the true husband, coming upon the scene, may retract the alienations of his property, and not only the parcels sold, but may also recover the fruits gathered and received by the purchasers since the time of the contracts. For the decision of which doubt, it must be presupposed that anyone may freely sell not only his own property, of which he is master and owner, but also the property of another; and the sale is good and valid <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup> — in so far, however, as concerns the prejudice of the seller, who by this contract is bound to deliver the thing sold, or to pay damages, and further, if the parcel is evicted by a third party, to warrant and indemnify the purchaser <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. But to the detri

notes.original: l. rem alienam. D. d. cõ trah. empt.
notes.gloss: Ulpian: there is no doubt that a man may sell a thing belonging to another; the sale is valid, though the thing may be taken from the buyer.

notes.citation: Digest 19.1.11 pr. (De actionibus empti venditi, l. Ex empto, at the beginning)
notes.original: l ex empt. au commence ment D. de actio. empe.
notes.gloss: Ulpian on what the buyer may claim from the seller by the action on purchase: delivery, or damages, and warranty against eviction.
